extracted.intended_audience: public water systems (PWSs), State/Territory/Tribal primacy agencies, drinking water regulators, and stakeholders/commenters on the proposed perchlorate NPDWR
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance for the EPA's proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for perchlorate, covering monitoring, use of historical data, sampling methods, consumer notification and CCR requirements, treatment technology lists (BATs/SSCTs), primacy/State requirements, exemptions/extensions, funding/assistance, and the HRRCA/benefit-cost analysis requirements. Intended to direct regulated systems, primacy agencies, and public commenters on compliance and implementation expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of previously collected data for initial monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: States can allow systems to use perchlorate data collected after January 1, 2021, to satisfy the initial monitoring requirements in 40 CFR 141.23(c)(10)(i)-(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify, a system must either have collected the same number of samples as required for initial monitoring (i.e., two or four depending on system size and type) or have data collected under a State monitoring requirement. The EPA proposes a cut-off date of approximately six years prior to the beginning of the initial monitoring period (January 1, 2021) to ensure recent data are used. State approval is required to apply previously collected data; the Agency is seeking comment on alternative cut-off dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite sampling allowance and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 40 CFR 141.23(a)(4) a State may permit compositing of up to five equal-volume samples (composite sampling) where the reported concentration reflects the average of contributing entry points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite sampling can reduce analytical costs because a single composite is analyzed. If the composite concentration is greater than or equal to the MCL divided by the number of samples in the composite, the system must take follow-up individual samples at each sampling point included in the composite and analyze them separately. Example: at a 20 µg/L MCL, a five-sample composite with concentration ≥4 µg/L triggers follow-up sampling at each entry point. The EPA expects many systems will have perchlorate far below the MCL and compositing is a potential cost-reduction method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer Confidence Report (CCR) reporting requirements for perchlorate
rubrics_metrics.description: Community Water Systems (CWSs) must include perchlorate information in the CCR per 40 CFR part 141, subpart O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with other detected regulated contaminants, CCR content must include the MCL, MCLG, range of detected levels, highest detected level used for compliance, and likely sources of perchlorate. If there is an MCL violation, the CCR must also include information about the violation, potential adverse health effects of perchlorate, and actions taken by the system to address the violation. EPA is proposing mandatory health effects language for perchlorate to be listed in appendix A to subpart O.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Notification (PN) requirements and tiers for perchlorate
rubrics_metrics.description: Public water systems must give public notice for violations of NPDWRs and other situations under 40 CFR 141.201; the PN Rule defines three tiers of PN based on seriousness and potential adverse health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is proposing revisions to 40 CFR 141.202 to apply PN requirements to the proposed perchlorate rule and to include mandatory health effects language for perchlorate in appendix A of subpart Q. Violations of the perchlorate MCL are proposed to be designated as Tier 1. EPA is proposing Tier 3 PN for perchlorate monitoring and testing procedure violations (consistent with other IOCs). The Agency requests comment on selecting Tier 1 rather than Tier 2 for MCL exceedances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for Tier 1 PN designation for perchlorate MCL exceedance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposes Tier 1 PN for MCL exceedances because the most sensitive adverse health effect is decreased IQ in offspring from short-term exposure during critical developmental periods (first trimester), making timely notification important for at-risk populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes potential benefits to a broader population (e.g., females of reproductive age). EPA also acknowledges implementation challenges for systems in complying with Tier 1 PN and solicits comment on the tier selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to adopt treatment or other strategies when exceeding MCL
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that exceed the proposed perchlorate MCL would need to adopt new treatment or another strategy to reduce perchlorate to meet the MCL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-treatment compliance options identified include blending existing sources, replacing a contaminated source (e.g., new well), and purchasing compliant water from another system. States may allow variances/exemptions in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA duty to list Best Available Technologies (BATs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When establishing an MCL, SDWA section 1412(b)(4)(E)(i) requires EPA to “list the technology, treatment techniques, and other means which the Administrator finds to be feasible for purposes of meeting [the MCL],” referred to as BATs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BATs are not mandatory for systems to implement for rule compliance but are used by States to establish conditions for source water variances. EPA must also identify Small System Compliance Technologies (SSCTs) under SDWA section 1412(b)(4)(E)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria defining Best Available Technologies (BATs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA identifies BATs as those meeting: (1) capability of a high removal efficiency, (2) history of full-scale operation, (3) general geographic applicability, (4) compatibility with other water treatment processes, (5) ability to bring all the water in a system into compliance, and (6) reasonable cost basis for large and medium water systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used review of treatment and cost literature to assess technologies against these criteria and proposes listing technologies that meet them as BATs for perchlorate removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed BATs for perchlorate
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is proposing to list the following technologies as BATs for removal of perchlorate from drinking water: Ion exchange; Biological treatment; Reverse osmosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposal is based on review of treatment and cost literature. Further details on each BAT and non-treatment options are in the referenced BAT/SSCT report (USEPA, 2025c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to identify Small System Compliance Technologies (SSCTs)
rubrics_metrics.description: SDWA requires the Agency to identify SSCTs—more affordable treatment technologies or other means that can achieve compliance with the MCL for small systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA identified SSCTs based on analysis of treatment effectiveness and affordability. For perchlorate the SSCTs include a point-of-use (POU) version of reverse osmosis in addition to ion exchange, biological treatment, and reverse osmosis. EPA applied its 1998 affordability methodology and supplemental analyses using alternative metrics to demonstrate affordability implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSCT effectiveness and affordability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: An SSCT must meet effectiveness requirements and be affordable for the small system size categories defined in SDWA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes POU reverse osmosis meets effectiveness for small systems; EPA is not aware of any point-of-entry (POE) devices certified for perchlorate removal or POU devices certified for perchlorate removal using technologies other than reverse osmosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date and initial monitoring completion
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposes setting the compliance date three years after the date of publication of the final rule; water systems would complete all initial monitoring by the compliance date and start compliance monitoring on a schedule based on initial monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA acknowledges logistical challenges in aligning with the Synthetic Minor Frequency (SMF) cycle and is seeking comment on whether a sooner compliance date is practicable. See discussion of extensions and exemptions for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy requirements for States/Territories/Tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain primacy, States must adopt regulations no less stringent than Federal NPDWRs and meet requirements under SDWA section 1413 (adopt and implement enforcement procedures, keep records, issue variances/exemptions under appropriate conditions, and have emergency plans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To implement the perchlorate rule, States would be required to adopt revisions at least as stringent as the specified CFR provisions (e.g., 40 CFR 141.6; 141.23; 141.51; 141.62; appendices for CCR and PN; 40 CFR 142.62). Under 40 CFR 142.12(b), primacy program revisions must be submitted within two years of promulgation (with possible extension up to two years). EPA must approve/deny within 90 days after a submission is complete; interim primacy may apply in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: State monitoring plan and waiver/waiver-review procedures as part of primacy package
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 40 CFR 142.16(e)(2), primacy revision applications must include a monitoring plan enforceable under State law assuring all systems complete required initial monitoring; if a State allows waivers under 40 CFR 141.23(c), the primacy package must describe procedures and criteria the State will use to review waiver applications and issue waiver determinations (40 CFR 142.16(e)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must also explain their initial monitoring schedules, how schedules ensure compliance with the MCL and monitoring requirements, and the timeframe in which new systems will be required to demonstrate compliance (40 CFR 142.16(k)).

rubrics_metrics.name: State recordkeeping requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: States with primacy must keep records of analytical results to determine compliance, system inventories, sanitary surveys, State approvals, vulnerability and waiver determinations, monitoring requirements, monitoring frequency decisions, enforcement actions, and issuance of variances and exemptions (40 CFR 142.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is not proposing changes to these recordkeeping requirements and they would apply to perchlorate as with other regulated contaminants.

rubrics_metrics.name: State reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: States must report information under 40 CFR 142.15 regarding violations, variances and exemptions, enforcement actions, and general operations of State public water supply programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is not proposing changes to reporting requirements but the perchlorate MCL could increase the frequency of reporting by certain States. See Paperwork Reduction Act discussion for additional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and extensions authority and criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: SDWA section 1412(b)(10) allows EPA or the State to allow up to two additional years for compliance with an MCL if additional time is necessary for capital improvements; SDWA section 1416 permits exemptions for PWSs meeting specified criteria providing up to three years beyond the 1412(b)(10) extension, and special provisions authorize up to three additional two-year period exemptions (not to exceed six years) for systems serving 3,300 people or fewer in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may grant exemptions upon finding: (1) compelling factors (including economic) make the system unable to comply or develop alternative source; (2) the system was in operation on the effective date (new systems only if no reasonable alternative source); (3) granting the exemption will not result in an unreasonable risk to health; and (4) management or restructuring changes cannot reasonably be made to achieve compliance or improve water quality. EPA is not proposing a nationwide two-year extension but states can make individualized extension determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and technical assistance availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding sources and technical assistance exist to assist systems comply with a perchlorate NPDWR, subject to appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential resources include the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF), EPA grant programs that provide technical assistance and funding, and the EPA's Water Technical Assistance (WaterTA) programs and initiatives to help small systems assess challenges, implement solutions, build capacity, and develop funding applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health Risk Reduction and Cost Analysis (HRRCA) required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: SDWA section 1412(b)(3)(C)(i) requires the EPA to prepare an HRRCA for any NPDWR that includes an MCL; the HRRCA must include specified elements (I–VII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements: (I) quantifiable/nonquantifiable health risk reduction benefits with a factual basis; (II) benefits from reductions in co-occurring contaminants attributable solely to compliance; (III) quantifiable/nonquantifiable costs solely resulting from compliance; (IV) incremental costs and benefits for each alternative MCL; (V) effects on the general population and identified subpopulations at greater risk; (VI) any increased health risk that may occur as a result of compliance (including co-occurring contaminant risks); and (VII) other relevant factors including quality/extent of information and uncertainties. EPA's Economic Analysis uses a 35-year analysis window and SafeWater CBX to estimate costs/benefits and discusses uncertainty and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit-cost determination requirement and statutory consideration of alternative MCLs
rubrics_metrics.description: SDWA section 1412(b)(4)(C) requires the Administrator to publish a determination whether the benefits of the MCL justify the costs based on the HRRCA; SDWA section 1412(b)(6)(A) allows promulgation of an MCL that maximizes health risk reduction benefits at a cost justified by the benefits after notice and comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the proposed perchlorate NPDWR, the Administrator determined the quantified and nonquantifiable benefits do not justify the costs at the evaluated MCLs due to significant monitoring and administrative costs and infrequent occurrence of perchlorate at levels of health concern. EPA nevertheless proposes and seeks comment on MCLs of 20 µg/L, 40 µg/L, and 80 µg/L and evaluated net benefits at multiple discount rates and uncertainty bounds; EPA explains how monitoring/administrative costs limit improvements in net benefits when raising the MCL.
